entries.mechanism: A count is a finish line and the numeral is scanned first; the second beat states the payoff, not a teaching promise.

N.rule: exactly the number of payoff slides (gate C6)

things.rule: concrete and countable: tools, habits, rules, templates

outcome.rule: a result the reader wants in plain verbs; never "learn" or "discover"

entries.slide2: Pay off at once with item 1 (or the strongest item) plus one proof, then bridge to item 2 and hint that the best one comes later.

examples.text: 7 small habits… that help you study faster
5 free apps… that help you control your spending

entries.mechanism: A fixed, short time frame makes the list feel doable today, which is what turns a save into an action.

N.rule: exactly the number of payoff slides

things.rule: tasks the reader can do, not topics to read about

time.rule: a real duration, short enough to believe

payoff.rule: the moment or result the time box protects

entries.slide2: Start with step 1 and its time cost; the counter on every slide shows the time left.

examples.text: 5 things in 10 minutes… before you post anything

entries.mechanism: Names who the list is for, so the right reader self-selects and the post is easy to send to a colleague.

N.rule: exactly the number of payoff slides

things.rule: rules, mistakes, tools, numbers: something that can be listed

entries.slide2: Open with the first item as a rule in one line and one example; keep the same audience word on the counter.

examples.text: 4 rules every creator should know

entries.mechanism: Delivers the first list item with one line of payoff. Slide 2 becomes a second cover for readers who skipped slide 1.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

item.rule: the first (or strongest) list item, in a few words

payoff.rule: what it changes, in the reader's terms

entries.slide2: Bridge to item 2 with a small cliffhanger; the strongest item stays for the end.

examples.text:
No. 1: hardest subject first
The rest gets easier

entries.mechanism: Pairs a cost the reader already feels with a count of free substitutes. The most saved and shared carousel format on the maintainer's account.

evidence.note: 488 Arabic carousels, 157 creators: a numeral in line 1 beat the creator median 64% of the time vs 46% without one.

cost.rule: a recurring cost the audience recognises: a subscription, a tool, a course

N.rule: exactly the number of alternatives shown

result.rule: an honest, modest promise such as "cover most of the work"; never "same quality"

entries.slide2: Show the verdict for the first pair at once (paid tool vs its free alternative) in one line, then list the rest on the next slides.

examples.text: Paying for editing software? 5 free alternatives… cover most jobs
Paying for a design tool? 6 free alternatives… worth trying

name.en: A or B? I tried both

entries.mechanism: Two named options and a first-hand test give a clean either-or gap that the reader wants settled.

evidence.note: Information-gap theory: a specific, closable gap drives curiosity. No carousel lift measured.

skeleton.en: {A} or {B}? I tried both… here's the verdict

A.rule: the first option, specific enough to picture

B.rule: the second option, a real rival of A

entries.slide2: Give the winner for the first criterion immediately; do not hold the verdict back to the last slide.

examples.text: Morning gym or night gym? I tried both… here's the verdict

entries.mechanism: A purchase the audience is weighing plus a stated trial period turns a vague opinion into a tested verdict.

evidence.note: Information-gap theory: a specific, closable gap drives curiosity. No carousel lift measured.

skeleton.en: {product}… worth it? I used it for {time}

product.rule: something people pay for and hesitate over

time.rule: the real length of your trial

entries.slide2: Say the verdict in one line first (yes, no, only if...), then show the two or three reasons across the next slides.

examples.text: An iPad for studying… worth it? I used it for a year

name.en: The difference between A and B

entries.mechanism: Two things people confuse plus a count of differences promises a clear, finite explanation.

evidence.note: A visible count is a finish line and raises completion (goal-gradient effect).

A.rule: the first concept people mix up

N.rule: exactly the number of comparison slides

entries.slide2: State the biggest difference first as "A = ... / B = ..." in one line, then one difference per slide.

examples.text: Healthy eating vs dieting: the difference in 4 points

entries.mechanism: Gives the verdict of the first comparison round straight away, so the reader gets value before any explanation.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

entries.slide2: Bridge to the next criterion; leave the overall winner for the last slides.

examples.text:
Price round: the free tool wins
Same job, no subscription

entries.mechanism: Names the thing at risk and the moment it dies, but not the mistake itself; the mistake is the gap.

asset.rule: something the reader has made and cares about

event.rule: the moment that decides it (read, click, reply)

entries.slide2: Show the mistake in one concrete before example, then what it costs in the reader's terms; open the loop on the fix.

examples.text: This mistake kills your résumé… before page 2
This mistake kills your product photo… before the buyer clicks

entries.mechanism: A direct stop order on a habit the reader recognises, followed by a single consequence. One loss, never a pile of fears.

habit.rule: a habit in the present tense, as the reader would say it

consequence.rule: one concrete cost; no second fear

entries.slide2: Name the better habit in the first line, then show the cost of the old one with one example.

examples.text: Stop replying late… it's costing you clients

entries.mechanism: A counted list of mistakes aimed at one thing the reader values. The count promises a finish line; the cost makes it personal.

evidence.note: 488 Arabic carousels, 157 creators: a numeral in line 1 beat the creator median 64% of the time vs 46% without one.

N.rule: exactly the number of mistake slides

cost.rule: what is lost: time, effort, money, reach (one thing)

entries.slide2: Start with the most common mistake, one line on why it happens and one on the fix.

examples.text: 5 mistakes wasting your study time

name.en: Slide 2: the mistake and its cost

entries.mechanism: Names the mistake from the cover and shows what it costs in one concrete line, then turns toward the fix.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

mistake.rule: the mistake the cover pointed at, named exactly

cost.rule: what it costs, in one concrete line

entries.slide2: Bridge to the fix with a small promise ("the fix takes a minute").

examples.text:
The mistake: a generic first line
They close it before reading on

name.en: The worst advice I have heard

entries.mechanism: Quotes a piece of common advice and brands it the worst. The reader either agrees and wants the reason or disagrees and wants to argue.

advice.rule: advice people really give, quoted as they say it

field.rule: a field the audience works in

entries.slide2: State the better rule in big type first, mention the bad advice only once, then give one proof.

examples.text: "Work for free at first"? The worst advice in freelancing

entries.mechanism: A belief written as an equation, then a short denial. The reader wants to know when it fails.

belief.rule: a rule of thumb people believe, as an equation such as "more X = more Y"

entries.slide2: Say when it holds and when it breaks, in two short lines, with one example of each.

examples.text: More hours = better results? Not always

entries.mechanism: Attacks a habit that is praised, which breaks the expectation and makes the reader check their own habit.

skeleton.en: {habit}… can hurt more than it helps

habit.rule: a habit people admire (agree the verb gender with it)

entries.slide2: Say when it backfires with one concrete case, then what to do instead in one line.

examples.text: Staying up to study… can hurt more than it helps

entries.mechanism: A claim the audience half-believes, framed as a verdict. The slides run fact, myth, fallacy, fact: the myth is named once and the fact is bigger and last.

claim.rule: one claim people really repeat, stated plainly and checkable

entries.slide2: Give the verdict in one line (myth, fact, or "true only if...") and the single strongest reason.

examples.text: Paid courses beat YouTube… myth or fact?

entries.mechanism: Puts the correct rule first and bigger than the myth, which was named once on the cover. Corrections work best when the fact leads.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

fact.rule: the correct rule in a short line

proof.rule: one reason or example that proves it

entries.slide2: Bridge to the first myth-versus-fact pair; never repeat the myth in full.

examples.text:
Price from your first client…
That price anchors all the rest

entries.mechanism: A forward reference that names a real object (a setting, a feature) instead of a vague secret. Specific objects pass the hype lint; vague ones do not.

feature.rule: a named setting or feature in a named tool

payoff.rule: why it matters, in a few words; never "will change your life"

entries.slide2: Show the setting itself (a screenshot or a one-line path) on slide 2, then what it changes.

examples.text: A WhatsApp setting nobody touches… it saves you time

entries.mechanism: A shared grievance about a skill that was never taught. It names a concrete skill, so the reader wants the missing lesson.

skill.rule: a practical life or work skill ("money management", "email writing")

entries.slide2: Give lesson 1 immediately in one line, then tease that the most useful one is later.

examples.text: Why wasn't money management ever taught?

name.en: A question about a specific pain

entries.mechanism: Asks about a frustration the reader lives with, in their words. Question openers reach far on the maintainer's account but are saved less, so use it for reach and sends.

situation.rule: a recurring frustration, concrete enough to picture

entries.slide2: Answer with the root cause in one line and one proof, then bridge to the fix.

examples.text: Why does studying never stick?

entries.mechanism: Turns a question everyone silently asks into a shared moment. A top cover type on the maintainer's account; strong for sends because it feels like a conversation.

evidence.note: 'We all ask...' covers rank among the account's top carousels (small sample).

question.rule: a real either-or or how-to question; the slides answer it

entries.slide2: Answer the question in one line first, then show the reasoning; do not repeat the cover question.

examples.text: We all ask: start now, or wait until ready?
We all ask: pay for a course, or self-teach?

entries.mechanism: Asks whether a popular method works and says the author tested it. The trial period is the credibility; the verdict is the gap.

skeleton.en: Does {method} actually work? I tried it for {time}

method.rule: a named method, system or tactic people argue about

time.rule: the real length of the trial

entries.slide2: Give the verdict in one line (works, does not, works only if...) and the single measurable result.

examples.text: Does the Pomodoro method actually work? I tried it for a month

name.en: A method that produced a number

entries.mechanism: A small, specific change next to a precise result reads as research-backed. The figure must be the user's own and sourced.

number.rule: the user's own figure; needs a source or a "this is my number" tag (gate SRC1)

metric.rule: what was counted: saves, messages, orders

entries.slide2: Show the proof (screenshot or the before/after figures) before explaining; then name the single change.

examples.text: A tiny edit brought 120 messages… here's what I changed
examples.note: Illustrative figure: use your own and cite its source.

name.en: A result without the usual obstacle

entries.mechanism: Pairs a precise result with the obstacle the reader assumes is required. Proof and objection removal in one line.

result.rule: a counted result with its time frame, from the user's own work

obstacle.rule: the thing people think they need: ads, budget, a team, a camera

entries.slide2: Prove it with one screenshot or figure, then the first of the steps that replaced the obstacle.

examples.text: 30 new clients in a month… without paid ads
examples.note: Illustrative figure: use your own and cite its source.

entries.mechanism: Shows the before and after figures (or the screenshot) before explaining, which is what makes the cover's number believable.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

change.rule: the one change that made the difference

entries.slide2: Bridge to the first lever with the number of levers.

examples.text:
Proof: 15 messages, then 120
The change: the first line
examples.note: Illustrative figures: use your own and cite the source.

name.en: From X to Y in a period

entries.mechanism: Two concrete numbers and a time frame let the reader see their future self. Needs the user's real before and after.

before.rule: the starting figure with its unit

after.rule: the end figure with the same unit

entries.slide2: Show the before state with its one cause on slide 2, then the levers one per slide.

examples.text: From 15 orders to 60… in 90 days
examples.note: Illustrative figures: use your own and cite the source.

entries.mechanism: A visual before/after on a single change, with a promise that the difference is not the one expected. Works best with two real images.

skeleton.en: Before and after {change}… what changed isn't what you'd expect

change.rule: one visible change: a logo, a menu, a layout, a first line

entries.slide2: Show the before and after side by side on slide 2 and name the real difference in one line.

examples.text: Before and after a logo tweak… what changed isn't what you'd expect

entries.mechanism: Starts in the middle of an event and stops before the outcome. An unresolved sequence keeps people swiping; cold-open covers rank among the best on the maintainer's account.

event.rule: a plain action with a time span, written in the first person

surprise.rule: what was different on return; the slides explain how

entries.slide2: Give the stakes in one line (what was at risk) and start the first beat of the story.

examples.text: Closed the laptop for a week… came back to a growing account

name.en: I was about to quit… until

entries.mechanism: A near-quit moment followed by an unnamed turn. The reader stays to find out what changed.

evidence.note: Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

thing.rule: the page, shop, project or habit that nearly ended

turn.rule: the event that changed it, named only as an event

entries.slide2: State what was at stake in one line, then the first small step you took after the turn.

examples.text: I nearly closed my page… until a message arrived
I nearly stopped selling online… until a client asked a question

name.en: A client asked and I had no answer

entries.mechanism: A first-person moment of not knowing. Honest, specific, and it opens a loop on what the answer turned out to be.

evidence.note: Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

question.rule: a blunt question a real client could ask

aftermath.rule: the honest consequence, such as "I had no answer"

entries.slide2: Say what you answered back then, in one line, and promise the better answer that the carousel builds.

examples.text: A client asked: "Why should I pay you?"… I had no answer

name.ar: سلايد 2: إيه اللي كان على المحك

entries.mechanism: Gives the stakes of the cold open in one line, so the story has weight before the first beat starts.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

entries.slide2: Bridge into beat one of the story with a time marker.

examples.text:
On the line: my one-year-old page
and my last ad budget

entries.mechanism: Opens with the reader's situation, so the right person self-selects and the post is easy to send to a colleague. Generic "you" does not work; the identity must be specific.

identity.rule: a concrete situation or role ("starting out as a freelancer", "running a small shop")

N.rule: exactly the number of payoff slides

things.rule: what the reader gets: steps, ideas, templates, rules

entries.slide2: Repeat the identity in a short tag and give item 1 at once.

examples.text: Just starting out freelancing? 5 things to do first

entries.mechanism: A three-way identity quiz. Readers pick a type, tag a friend with another, and swipe to see the verdicts.
entries.slide2: Name the first type with one line of recognition and one line of advice; one type per slide.

examples.text: Which type are you? Procrastinator, perfectionist or sprinter?

entries.mechanism: A counted list of recognisable signs. Readers see themselves, send it to someone who fits, and swipe to check the count.

N.rule: exactly the number of sign slides

identity.rule: a state or role, in the reader's own words

entries.slide2: Give sign 1 with a one-line example, then keep the same sentence frame on every slide.

examples.text: 4 signs you're busy, not progressing

entries.mechanism: A counted pack of copy-ready prompts for one job. It is an asset the reader returns to, which is why this family earns the most saves on the maintainer's account.

N.rule: exactly the number of prompt slides

task.rule: the one job the prompts do ("for writing emails", "for studying")

benefit.rule: a modest, true benefit such as "ready to copy"; never a guaranteed result

entries.slide2: Put prompt 1 on slide 2, complete and copyable, with the result it gave; the rest follow one per slide.

examples.text: 6 prompts for writing emails… ready to copy
5 study prompts… any lesson summarised in minutes

entries.mechanism: Offers the personal checklist used before a real deadline. A reusable asset with a clear future moment, which is what makes people save it.

object.rule: the thing being checked: a design, a post, a contract

event.rule: the moment the check protects: delivery, publishing, signing

entries.slide2: Show the whole checklist as a single preview, then one item per slide with the reason it is on the list.

examples.text: My checklist for any design… before I deliver it
My checklist for any post… before I publish

name.en: My tool stack for one job

entries.mechanism: Shows the small set of tools used for one job. Tool packs lead the maintainer's saves; naming the job keeps the promise concrete.

N.rule: exactly the number of tool slides

price.rule: an honest price note, such as "all free" (check it is true)

entries.slide2: Name tool 1 with what it does in one line and a screenshot; list the remaining tools in order of use.

examples.text: 4 tools for all my editing… all free

entries.mechanism: A counted set of shortcuts or commands for one tool. The "keep it open next to your work" use is what drives saves.

N.rule: exactly the number of shortcut slides

tool.rule: one named tool the audience uses daily

benefit.rule: a modest benefit: saves time, worth memorising

entries.slide2: List the three most useful shortcuts at once as key combinations; the rest follow.

examples.text: 10 Excel shortcuts… that save you hours

entries.mechanism: Gives the first item of the pack at once, so the pack proves its value immediately. The full text sits in the body block, not in the headline.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

entries.slide2: Show the complete, copyable prompt in the body block of this slide, then bridge to prompt 2.

examples.text:
Prompt 1: angry-client reply
A calm, polite answer comes back

name.en: Today: news plus what it changes for you

entries.mechanism: A dated update paired with its effect on the reader. News wins reach on the day but earns few saves, so the effect is what makes it worth keeping.

skeleton.en: Today: {change}… here's what changes for you

change.rule: one dated, verifiable update from a named source

entries.slide2: State the fact in one line with its date and source, then the first thing the reader should do about it.

examples.text: Today: a delivery app update dropped… here's what changes for you
examples.note: Hypothetical event: use a real, dated, sourced update.

entries.mechanism: Compresses a story into a counted summary, which promises that the reader can stay informed in seconds.

N.rule: exactly the number of point slides

entries.slide2: Open with point 1, the one that affects most readers, with its source.

examples.text: The new update: 3 points to know
examples.note: Hypothetical event: use a real, dated, sourced update.

name.en: If you [identity]… this news concerns you

entries.mechanism: Pre-qualifies the readers an update affects, which turns a general news item into a personal alert that is easy to send.

audience.rule: the people the update changes things for

entries.slide2: Say exactly what changes for this audience in one line, then the date it starts.

examples.text: If you sell online… this update affects you
examples.note: Hypothetical event: use a real, dated, sourced update.

name.en: Slide 2: the news in one line

entries.mechanism: States the fact in one line and the single change that matters most. News readers want the facts first, then the effect.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

fact.rule: the verifiable fact with its source and date

effect.rule: the one change that matters most to the reader

entries.slide2: Bridge to what the reader should do next.

examples.text:
The news: a delivery app update
Biggest change: how you pay
examples.note: Hypothetical event: use a real, dated, sourced update.

name.en: Imagine a simple input and a full result

entries.mechanism: A short scene where one small action produces a finished result. A visualisable scene sticks better than a claim, and "imagine" covers rank second by shares on the maintainer's account.

input.rule: a small, easy action the reader can picture

result.rule: the finished outcome that comes back

entries.slide2: Show that it is real: the actual input and the actual result side by side, then how it works in one line.

examples.text: Imagine a phone photo… that becomes a studio shot
Imagine sending a voice note… and getting a weekly plan back

entries.mechanism: A what-if scenario about the reader's own work. It sets a desire and a gap in one line, and works for launches and offers as well as for news.

evidence.note: Information-gap theory: a specific, closable gap drives curiosity. No carousel lift measured.

scenario.rule: a desirable or surprising situation in the reader's work, written in the present

entries.slide2: Answer the what-if concretely on slide 2 with one real or modelled example, then show how to get there.

examples.text: What if your calendar filled itself?

entries.mechanism: A morning scene that lets the reader feel the finished state before any explanation. Strong for soft launches and tool posts.

state.rule: the finished state the reader wants (work done, week planned)

entries.slide2: Break the scene into its parts: what was done for you and what you still do yourself.

examples.text: Imagine waking up… and the week's content is ready

entries.mechanism: Turns the imagined scene into proof: the real input and the real result side by side.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

claim.rule: a short statement that it already works

proof.rule: what the slide shows as evidence

entries.slide2: Bridge to how it is done: step one in one line.

examples.text:
Not fiction: it works today
Input and result, side by side

name.ar: إزاي تعمل كذا من غير كذا
name.en: How to do X without Y

entries.mechanism: States the result and removes the obstacle the reader assumes. Objection removal is the whole mechanism.

result.rule: a result the reader wants, as a verb phrase

obstacle.rule: the obstacle they assume is required

entries.slide2: Give step 1 at once and say why the obstacle was never needed.

examples.text: Learn a language without courses

entries.mechanism: Names the doubt the reader holds about themselves (beginner, busy, no talent) and answers it before it is voiced.

result.rule: what the carousel teaches, as a plain promise

objection.rule: the reader's self-doubt, in their words

entries.slide2: Show the smallest first step a beginner can do today.

examples.text: Learn editing even if you're new

name.en: I tested N and ranked them

entries.mechanism: Proof of work plus a ranking. People swipe to find who is number one, and the list is easy to save as a buying guide.

N.rule: exactly the number of items you really tested

entries.slide2: Reveal the last place first, with the one reason it failed; number one stays for the end.

examples.text: I tested 8 time-management apps… here's the ranking
I took 10 design courses… ranked by usefulness

entries.mechanism: The ordering is the promise. It tells the reader the list is ranked, so the last slide is where the payoff sits.

N.rule: exactly the number of ranked slides

things.rule: items that can honestly be ranked

entries.slide2: Start from the worst item with one line on why it ranks last.

examples.text: Worst to best: 6 ways to study

name.en: Tried many, few were worth it

entries.mechanism: A filter story: many tested, few kept. The shortlist is the reader's saved time and the gap is which ones made it.

skeleton.en: I tried {N} {things}… only {M} earned a spot

N.rule: the number you really tried

M.rule: the number you recommend; it equals the payoff slides

entries.slide2: Show the quick cut: why most failed in one line, then item 1 of the keepers.

examples.text: I tried 12 writing tools… only 3 earned a spot

entries.mechanism: Reveals last place first with the reason it failed, so the reader gets a verdict at once and swipes for the winner.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

entries.slide2: Bridge up the ranking one place at a time; number one is the last slide before the call to action.

examples.text:
Last place: the complicated app
I spent more time learning it

entries.mechanism: A single striking figure stands alone, then a short context. The isolation does the attracting; the figure must be sourced.

number.rule: one sourced figure with its unit; the user's own data or a cited source

context.rule: what the figure measures, in plain words

entries.slide2: Cite the source and date in a line, then say what the figure means for the reader.

examples.text: 180 saves… from a one-hour design
examples.note: Illustrative figure: use your own and cite its source.

entries.mechanism: Two figures that seem to clash (many followers, few interactions) make the reader ask which one matters. Both figures need sources.

a.rule: the big, impressive figure with its unit

b.rule: the small, telling figure with its unit

entries.slide2: Explain which of the two figures counts and why, with its source.

examples.text: 20,000 followers… and just 12 interactions
examples.note: Illustrative figures: use your own and cite the source.

name.en: The problem is not… it is…

entries.mechanism: Moves the blame from what the audience assumes to the real, fixable cause. The cover states the shift and slide 2 proves it. The strongest contrast family on the maintainer's account.

evidence.note: A broken expectation pulls attention and creates curiosity (psychology literature); not measured on carousels.

root.rule: the real cause: concrete and fixable, and proven by the slides

entries.slide2: Show the root with one proof (a before example), then open a loop to the fix.

examples.text: Your problem isn't time… it's priorities
Your problem isn't the competition… it's your offer

entries.mechanism: The shortest form of the contrast: two nouns, one pivot. Works when the audience already agrees on X and the post replaces it.

evidence.note: A broken expectation pulls attention and creates curiosity (psychology literature); not measured on carousels.

Y.rule: the thing that actually decides it (agree the pronoun with its gender)

entries.slide2: Prove Y with one before-and-after pair, then show how to improve Y first.

examples.text: It's not the camera that matters… it's the lighting
It's not followers that sell… it's trust

entries.mechanism: Grants that X matters, then adds the missing condition. Less hostile than a flip, so it travels well for MSA and brand voices.

X.rule: a quality people rely on (talent, product quality, effort)

condition.rule: the missing piece, stated as its absence

entries.slide2: Name the missing piece on slide 2 with one example of someone who had X but lacked it.

examples.text: Talent isn't enough… if there's no system
Product quality isn't enough… if the photo is weak

name.en: X does not mean… it means…

entries.mechanism: Redefines a loaded word. The old meaning is named once and the new one is the promise the slides prove.

term.rule: a loaded word that is concrete enough to picture: experience, productivity, branding

entries.slide2: Show the new definition in action with one person or case that fits it.

examples.text: Experience doesn't mean more years… it means more attempts
Productivity doesn't mean doing more… it means doing the right thing

name.en: Slide 2: the real cause and its proof

entries.mechanism: Names the root cause that the cover moved the blame to and gives one proof, then opens a loop to the fix.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

root.rule: the root cause from the cover

proof.rule: one concrete proof, drawn from the reader's world

entries.slide2: Bridge to the fix: "and the fix takes minutes" or the first step.

examples.text:
The real cause: your priorities
A trivial task ate your day

entries.mechanism: Points at a contradiction in the reader's own routine. The laugh of recognition makes it shareable and the gap is the fix.

fast.rule: the quick action with its short time, as a bare verb (the skeleton adds the dialect prefix)

slow.rule: the slow, wasteful action with its long time, as a bare verb

entries.slide2: Show where the long time goes (one cause) and the shortcut in one line.

examples.text: Designing a slide takes an hour… finding the idea takes a week?

entries.mechanism: Contrasts what the reader spends on with the neglected thing that cancels the spend. One irony per cover.

spend.rule: something the reader pays for or invests in

entries.slide2: Show the neglected thing as the real lever, with one number or example from the reader's world.

examples.text: You pay for ads… then leave your profile unfinished?

entries.mechanism: Interrupts a decision the reader is about to make with a short set of questions. A reusable checklist, so it is saved.

decision.rule: a real decision with money or time at stake

N.rule: exactly the number of question slides

entries.slide2: Ask question 1 at once, with why it matters in one line.

examples.text: Before you change jobs… answer 4 questions

entries.mechanism: A pre-publish checklist aimed at creators. Concrete, reusable and easy to send to a teammate.

content.rule: the kind of content: any post, a reel, an ad

N.rule: exactly the number of check slides

entries.slide2: Give check 1 as a yes/no question with the cost of getting it wrong.

examples.text: Before you post anything… check 5 things

entries.mechanism: Asks the first check question immediately with the cost of the wrong answer. The reader starts doing the checklist on slide 2.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

question.rule: a yes/no question the reader can answer in seconds

entries.slide2: Bridge to question 2.

examples.text:
Question 1: will you use it?
If not, keep your money

entries.mechanism: A realistic situation and two options that both feel defensible. Readers pick a side and send it to someone who disagrees.

situation.rule: a realistic dilemma from the audience's work or life

entries.slide2: Give your own answer in one line and the principle behind it, then invite a different view.

examples.text: If a friend copies your idea… confront or stay quiet?

entries.mechanism: A fairness question with two fair-looking parties. It starts the argument in the comments and travels by send.

thing.rule: a cost, a mistake or a risk

entries.slide2: Show a real or modelled case and the split you would choose.

examples.text: Who should bear the design mistake: the client or the designer?

entries.mechanism: Pairs a credible identity with a view the audience would not expect from it. The identity gives the stance weight.

stance.rule: a view that cuts against what that role is expected to say

entries.slide2: Back the stance with one case from your own work, then the rule you follow.

examples.text: I'm a designer… I say write first, design second

entries.mechanism: Flags a view as a minority position, which invites agreement and pushback in equal measure. Keep it specific and defensible.

opinion.rule: a specific view you can defend with a case

entries.slide2: State the reason in one line and the one condition under which you would change your mind.

examples.text: Unpopular opinion: working from home isn't for everyone

name.en: I am for X… but not at the cost of Y

entries.mechanism: A balanced stance that takes a side without attacking the other. Safe for brands and good for send because both camps see themselves.

skeleton.en: I'm for {X}… not at the cost of {Y}

X.rule: the trend or tool you support

Y.rule: the value you will not trade for it

entries.slide2: Say where the line is, with one case on each side of it.

examples.text: I'm for AI… not at the cost of quality

entries.mechanism: Years in the field give the claim weight, and "stopped doing" implies hard-won lessons. The years and the count are the user's own facts.

skeleton.en: After {N} years in {field}… I stopped doing {M} things

N.rule: your real years in the field (a user fact; needs a source tag)

M.rule: exactly the number of stop-doing slides

entries.slide2: Name the first thing you stopped and what you do instead, in two short lines.

examples.text: After 8 years in design… I stopped doing 3 things
examples.note: Illustrative years: use your own and tag them as yours.

entries.mechanism: Condenses years of work into one lesson stated as a surprising claim. The lesson is the gap; the slides give the evidence.

N.rule: your real years (a user fact; needs a source tag)

lesson.rule: a counter-intuitive lesson you can back with a case

entries.slide2: Give the lesson's first proof as a short before-and-after from your own work.

examples.text: 5 years of freelancing taught me: cheap is expensive
examples.note: Illustrative years: use your own and tag them as yours.

name.ar: إنت شايف النتيجة… أنا شايف اللي وراها
name.en: You see the result… I see what is behind it

entries.mechanism: Contrasts the visible result with the unseen work or decisions behind it. It builds authority and invites the save of a behind-the-scenes process.

skeleton.en: You see {result}… I see {N} {things} behind it

N.rule: exactly the number of hidden-layer slides

entries.slide2: Reveal the first hidden layer with one real example from the work.

examples.text: You see a successful post… I see 14 decisions behind it

name.en: A simple result with hidden work

entries.mechanism: A modest-looking result and a hint of the work nobody saw. Credibility through effort, and a natural step-by-step process carousel.

time.rule: the real effort: a week, many drafts

entries.slide2: Show the first stage of the hidden work with a screenshot or draft.

examples.text: A simple carousel… a week of unseen work

entries.mechanism: Reveals the first hidden layer of work straight away, with the surprise that most of the work is invisible.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

layer.rule: the first stage of the hidden work

surprise.rule: the part of it people never see

entries.slide2: Bridge to layer 2 with the time it took.

examples.text:
Layer 1: choosing the idea
Most ideas get cut before design

entries.mechanism: Gives away the working file you really use. Free value first builds the reason to follow. A keyword-to-DM call to action is allowed only when the file reaches the reader instantly.

asset.rule: a real file, template or checklist you use

how.rule: how you use it, in the first person

entries.slide2: Show what is inside (two or three items) and how to get it. State the delivery path honestly.

examples.text: The budget template I use… free

name.en: What you asked for is ready

entries.mechanism: Frames a launch as the answer to real requests. It works only when people did ask, and it turns existing demand into a clear next step.

skeleton.en: What you kept asking for: {product} is ready

product.rule: the thing you launch, named plainly (agree the verb gender with it)

entries.slide2: Quote or paraphrase one real request, then show what the product does in one line.

examples.text: What you kept asking for: the phone filming guide is ready

entries.mechanism: Real scarcity: a true seat limit or an invite-only wave. Never invent a limit; the figure is the user's own and must be stated.

product.rule: the workshop, cohort or beta the places belong to

N.rule: the real number of places left (a user fact)

entries.slide2: Say what the places include and the date the doors close, both true and checkable.

examples.text: The writing workshop… 20 seats only
examples.note: Use only if the limit is real; state your actual number.

name.en: A bundle with everything in it

entries.mechanism: Packs several useful assets into one named bundle, so the offer reads as one clear purchase rather than a list of parts.

N.rule: the real count of items inside

entries.slide2: List what is inside in one line and show the single most useful item.

examples.text: The starter bundle: 10 templates, a month plan

entries.mechanism: Shows what the offer contains on slide 2 so the soft sell starts from value, not from a pitch.

evidence.note: Non-swipers are often re-served the carousel from slide 2 (Oct 2024): slide 2 works as a second cover.
Practitioners agree: slide 1 builds intrigue, slide 2 resolves it and opens a bigger loop.

contents.rule: what is really in the offer

access.rule: how the reader opens or uses it

entries.slide2: Bridge to the best single item shown in full.

examples.text:
Inside: 10 templates, a month plan
Edit them on your phone

name.en: You do this… it does that

entries.mechanism: Splits the work between the reader and the product in two short beats. The reader keeps the part they enjoy and the product takes the chore. Needs honest scope.

youdo.rule: the part that stays with the reader

itdoes.rule: the part the product takes over, stated modestly

entries.slide2: Show the handover in one real example: what the reader gives and what comes back.

examples.text: You tell us the idea… we build the slides

name.en: From one input to ready outputs

entries.mechanism: Shows the multiplication a product offers: one input, several finished outputs. The count must match what the product really returns.

input.rule: the small thing the reader provides

N.rule: the real number of outputs the product returns

entries.slide2: Show one input and its outputs side by side, then the time it took.

examples.text: From an idea… to 8 ready slides

entries.mechanism: Replaces a chore with the product's way in one swap. The old way is named so the reader recognises the pain it removes.
entries.slide2: Show the old way and the new way side by side, with the time or steps saved.

examples.text: Instead of a blank page… start from a ready template

name.en: A small delay that costs a lot

entries.mechanism: Names a small, common delay and the one thing it can cost. Use one loss, never a pile. Any figure about lost sales needs a source.

evidence.note: Soft-sell pattern from a creator's hook bank and ad lines; untested on carousels.

delay.rule: a small, concrete delay in the reader's work

loss.rule: the one thing it can cost

entries.slide2: Show the cost with a source or the reader's own data, then the one change that prevents it.

examples.text: 30 minutes before you reply… the price is the client
examples.note: Illustrative: back any figure with your data or a source.

name.ar: كل أسبوع من غير كذا… بتخسر
name.en: Every week without X… you lose

entries.mechanism: A rhythm of loss: each period without the fix costs something. Keep it to one loss and never frighten; the fix must be in the slides.

evidence.note: Soft-sell pattern from a creator's hook bank and ad lines; untested on carousels.

loss.rule: the one thing that is lost

entries.slide2: Show the loss as a before example and the smallest fix that stops it.

examples.text: Every week without a content plan… you lose followers
examples.note: General claim: back it with your data or a source.
